title: When does memoization actually beat tabulation? (not a homework question)
author: off_by_one
body:
Every DP explanation I read says "top-down is memoization, bottom-up is tabulation, pick whichever" and then moves on, which is useless the moment you actually care.

So here's what I've actually hit:

- **Memoization wins when the state space is sparse.** If your recurrence only ever touches a fraction of the table, tabulation fills the whole thing for nothing. Coin change with a huge amount and three coin values is the obvious one.
- **Tabulation wins when you need the whole table anyway**, or when the recursion depth would blow the stack. I've hit `RecursionError` on a 10^5 chain in Python more than once.
- Tabulation also lets you do the rolling-array trick and drop to O(n) space. You basically can't do that top-down because you don't control the order.

What I'm less sure about: is there a case where memoization is *faster* on a dense state space? The hash lookups should lose to array indexing every time, but I keep seeing people claim otherwise.

replies.author: tail_recursive
replies.body:
> is there a case where memoization is faster on a dense state space

Yes, if the transition is expensive enough that the lookup cost disappears into the noise. I had one where each state needed a small matrix multiply, and the memo overhead was maybe 2% of total runtime. At that point you pick whichever one you can read.

Also worth saying: use an array for the memo, not a dict, if your states are small integers. `memo = [None] * n` beats `{}` by a lot and you keep the top-down shape.

replies.author: midnight_compiler
replies.body:
The stack depth thing is the one that bites people in interviews. Python defaults to 1000 frames. `sys.setrecursionlimit` doesn't raise the actual C stack so you can still segfault, it just moves where you crash.

If you like the top-down shape but need the depth, write it as an explicit stack. Ugly but it doesn't fall over.

replies.author: heap_of_trouble
replies.body: Adding one: tabulation makes the dependency order explicit, which is how you find out your recurrence is wrong. Top-down will happily recurse into a cycle and you get infinite recursion instead of "this isn't a DAG". Caught a bad state definition that way last week.
